Chinese President Xi Jinping will pay a state visit to the United States from September 23 to 25, meeting US President Donald Trump for talks. President Xi expressed hope on Monday that younger generations will advance Sino-US cooperation and foster mutual understanding, responding to students from 10 US universities who attended a youth exchange program in China. The leaders are expected to discuss issues including trade, artificial intelligence, and broader bilateral relations, even as Breitbart News refers to Xi Jinping as a "genocidal dictator."

President Vladimir Putin's United Russia party secured a record supermajority in the State Duma election, winning 355 of the 450 seats. Electoral chief Ella Pamfilova announced the preliminary results, which surpass the party's previous record of 343 seats.

Paramount settled a lawsuit with a coalition of 12 Democratic state attorneys general, clearing the path for its $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The agreement binds Paramount to operate Warner Bros. Studios and Paramount Pictures separately, committing the combined company to release at least 30 films annually. A board will also be created to ensure the editorial independence of CNN, though advocates like the Committee for the First Amendment and Free Press expressed disappointment.

The Trump administration prepares sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), measures that could cut the court off from much of the global financial system. Proposed sanctions would bar most transactions involving the ICC after a six-to-seven-month wind-down period, potentially preventing the court from transacting in US dollars or protecting witnesses. The United States objects to the ICC's arrest warrants for Israeli officials and past investigations into American military actions in Afghanistan.

President Donald Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani will meet on Monday at Gracie Mansion, their third in-person encounter. The meeting occurs ahead of the United Nations General Assembly, where Trump is traveling to New York City this week.

The United States and Denmark reached a security deal concerning Greenland, which will develop a military presence on the territory and block Washington's adversaries from building bases. Shares of US-listed companies exposed to Greenland surged on Monday, with Greenland Energy soaring 159% and Greenland Mines up over 200%. Danish officials state the deal places Arctic security under NATO's responsibility.

President Donald Trump stated the Department of Justice and other US law enforcement agencies will rein in artificial intelligence risks "if they have to." Trump announced plans to create an "AI Force" and appoint an "AI czar," despite repeatedly calling potential dangers from AI a "hoax" in the past two weeks.

French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced plans to deepen economic and defense ties following a meeting in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon. The leaders discussed opportunities to share infrastructure in space and defense sectors, as well as cooperation in energy and telecommunications. Both leaders stated their countries are experiencing strained relations with the United States.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz vowed to keep his ruling coalition together after his Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party suffered defeats in two state elections. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the most votes in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, where the CDU failed to reach the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament. This marks the CDU's worst result in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern since 1945.

Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) fined Google 403 million euros (about $462 million) for improperly using users' location data. The DPC, Google's lead privacy regulator in Europe, gave Google's Irish subsidiary six months to bring its handling of location data into compliance with EU law. The inquiry found Google infringed the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) between May 2018 and February 2020.

## OPEN

## STORY 1 | China U-S Visit
A: Chinese President Xi Jinping will pay a state visit to the United States from Wednesday to Friday. He will meet U-S President Donald Trump for talks. This marks President Xi's first White House visit since two thousand fifteen. Chinese state media reports President Xi expressed hope that younger generations will advance cooperation. He says they should foster mutual understanding. President Xi made these remarks in a reply to a letter. Students from ten U-S universities sent the letter. They attended a youth exchange program in China earlier this month.
A: The leaders are expected to discuss several issues. These include trade, artificial intelligence, and broader bilateral relations. U-S First Lady Melania Trump will lead cultural diplomacy events. These include a visit with Peng Liyuan to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art. The visit will feature cultural exchanges. It will also include high-level discussions on bilateral relations.
A: Breitbart News frames the visit by referring to President Xi as a genocidal dictator. It highlights unethical behaviors from China. These include intellectual property theft and transnational repression. The Federalist emphasizes the risks of cooperating with China on A-I regulation. It cites past instances where China advanced its own interests. This happened at the expense of the United States. President Xi's comments precede his state visit. The visit will feature economic and security discussions.
B: President Xi's visit to Washington runs from September twenty-third to twenty-fifth.

## STORY 2 | Pakistan Detentions
B: In Pakistan, authorities have detained three sisters of former Prime Minister Imran Khan. The detentions occurred ahead of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's planned September twenty-seventh protest. Aleema Khan was detained on Sunday. She was transferred to Kot Lakhpat jail. On Monday, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi were also detained. They face detention for thirty days under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance. They were also moved to Kot Lakhpat jail.
B: The Lahore Deputy Commissioner's office issued the detention orders. The office cites that the sisters were prejudicial to public safety. It says they were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The office also says they were involved in motivating workers to damage property. It says they were involved in creating law and order situations. Some outlets report Aleema Khan's detention on Sunday. Other outlets focus on the detention of Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi on Monday. Coverage varies in the specific reasons cited for detention. Some detail allegations of motivating workers. Others focus on general public order concerns.
A: A petition challenging the detentions has been filed.

## STORY 3 | Russia Election
A: President Vladimir Putin's United Russia party secured a record supermajority in the State Duma election. Officials announced the results on Monday. The election followed a three-day voting period. Electoral chief Ella Pamfilova states preliminary results show United Russia won three hundred fifty-five of the Duma's four hundred fifty seats. This result gives President Putin's party an increased supermajority. It surpasses its previous record of three hundred forty-three seats.
A: The Kremlin states this first parliamentary election since Moscow sent troops to Ukraine in two thousand twenty-two demonstrated Russian unity. It says Russians were united around President Putin. Ms. Pamfilova reports turnout was over fifty-nine percent. She thanked Russians for voting despite what she called psychological pressure on Russia. The election proceeded without parties opposing the conflict in Ukraine.
A: Daily Sabah and Le Monde lead with United Russia securing a record supermajority. They highlight its implications for constitutional changes. R-T focuses on the continuity of the State Duma's composition. This is despite domestic and international changes since the last election. The results solidify President Putin's political control.
B: The election concluded on Sunday.

## STORY 4 | Paramount Merger
B: To the markets, Paramount's owners made a series of concessions on Monday. This resolves a lawsuit that endangered the media company's one hundred eleven billion dollar takeover bid of Warner Bros. Discovery. The agreement binds Paramount to operate Warner Bros. Studios and Paramount Pictures separately. The combined company will release at least thirty films annually. It faces a thirty million dollar penalty per film if it falls short.
B: The deal also establishes a board. This board will insulate Warner's C-N-N from corporate intervention in newsroom decisions. Paramount pledged an additional one and a half billion dollar investment in California production over five years. It committed to keeping its headquarters in California. N-P-R and Reuters focus on Paramount making concessions to salvage the deal. They say settling with U-S states is a major step towards closing the merger. N-B-C News and HuffPost highlight the ongoing Block the Merger push by advocates. They report disappointment expressed by groups like the Committee for the First Amendment and Free Press.
A: The settlement was reached with a coalition of twelve Democratic state attorneys general.

## FINALLY | 13 | Google Fine
B: One more before Void Opinion. Ireland's Data Protection Commission fined Google four hundred three million euros on Monday. The fine is for improperly using users' location data. The D-P-C is Google's lead privacy regulator in Europe. It also gave Google's Irish subsidiary six months to comply with E-U law. The inquiry examined Google's practices from May twenty-fifth, two thousand eighteen, through February fourth, two thousand twenty. The D-P-C found Google handled location data unlawfully and unfairly. It says Google kept data too long and failed to explain its practices.

## CLOSE

opinion_text:
President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington this week for his first White House visit since 2015. President Trump will personally welcome him at Joint Base Andrews. The visit includes extensive ceremonial honors, with a full honor guard display by 479 military personnel. First Lady Melania Trump will lead cultural diplomacy events, including a visit with Peng Liyuan to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art.

The leaders are expected to discuss trade, artificial intelligence, and broader bilateral relations. This agenda unfolds against a backdrop of documented concerns. Accusations of intellectual property theft and transnational repression have been raised. Claims of "unethical behaviors" from China and references to a "genocidal dictator" have been made. Cooperation on artificial intelligence regulation carries risks; China has advanced its own interests at the expense of other nations in past instances.

We observe a striking asymmetry in this moment. President Xi has overseen a surge in China's trade. President Trump, by contrast, has struggled with falling approval ratings at home. The elaborate welcome and the focus on cooperation, despite the serious accusations and the power imbalance, suggest a prioritization of short-term diplomatic optics over long-term accountability. We must ask what fundamental principles are being sacrificed when such a grand reception is extended without clear commitments to address these systemic issues.

President Xi expressed hope that younger generations will advance Sino-US cooperation and foster mutual understanding. This sentiment, while aspirational, cannot overshadow the immediate realities. The mechanisms of intellectual property theft and transnational repression directly undermine the very trust required for genuine cooperation. The risks of unchecked AI collaboration could further entrench power imbalances, rather than level them.

The state visit offers a platform for dialogue. It also presents a moment of institutional choice. We believe the US government has a responsibility to ensure that ceremonial grandeur does not obscure the imperative to address documented human rights concerns and economic inequities. The cost of deferring accountability will ultimately be borne by those whose rights are suppressed and whose economic interests are undermined.
